svg.aria-label: One timeline from due date to premium receipt, cut into four in-grace buckets plus a lapsed tail, modelled by one ordinal chain instead of two chained models
svg.text: LAPSE IS NOT A SEPARATE EVENT. IT IS THE TAIL OF ONE NUMBER.
days from due date to premium receipt. Cut that one distribution and you get both answers at once.
due date
d31_grace
lapsed
day 0
grace period ends
no premium received
One model over these ordered buckets returns a calibrated distribution. P(lapse) is the last cell. Expected days is the shape of the first four.
THE USUAL DESIGN: TWO CHAINED MODELS
stage 1: will it lapse?
binary classifier, all rows
stage 2: how many days?
regression, PAID rows only
stage 2 trains on a shrunken, selected sample, so its errors
correlate with exactly what stage 1 got wrong
the two heads can disagree, and nothing reconciles them
measured: 10th of 11 models, below plain logistic regression
THIS DESIGN: ONE ORDINAL CHAIN
4 binary models, one per cumulative edge:
paid by day 7? by 15? by 30? by 45?
difference the CDF, enforce monotonicity, renormalise
each sub-model answers a question the business already asks out loud
the lapse tail is chain-consistent, and nothing is stitched at inference
one calibrated row per due date, summing to 1
measured: tied-best Brier 0.0761, PR-AUC 0.3804, fits in 12s
The honest headline: across 11 families the AUC spread is 0.802 to 0.818, and the gap to a prior-only baseline is 15x larger.
The design and the features are the decision. The algorithm is close to a rounding error, and the benchmark in this repo is what proves it.
